transcript:
**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 0):
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

**Jordan** (turn 1):
I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 2):
Yael’s glasses finished their journey onto her face, though she immediately looked over the top of them instead of through them.

“Whose vision — excellent first question, dangerous first question, the kind of question that sounds simple and then eats the furniture,” she said, already moving toward the rehearsal table and gesturing for the conversation to happen in motion. “The adaptation began with Rosa Delgado, and I want that sentence printed exactly that way if you use it — began with Rosa Delgado. Her language, her architecture, her refusal to make Medea digestible for people who like their tragedies pre-chewed.”

Her voice had steadied on Rosa’s name, the tempo still brisk but the edges cleaner, more deliberate.

“She set it in a 1970s commune because she understood that utopias are pressure cookers — everyone says family, everyone says collective, everyone says liberation, and then somebody is still washing the dishes, somebody is still holding the baby, somebody is still expected to be grateful for crumbs of power. That was Rosa’s great knife trick. She could take an ancient wound and make it look like it had been bleeding under your own floorboards.”

Yael pulled the glasses off again and let them hang from the chain, one hand already reaching for the marked-up script on the table.

“My vision, if we’re calling it that — and journalists do love a possessive noun — is in the staging. The rhythm. The bodies in the room. The way the chorus functions less like Greek citizens and more like people who have convinced themselves complicity is community. I’m responsible for the temperature of it, for keeping the production from becoming either museum piece or manifesto. Rosa built the house. I’m deciding where the audience has to stand while it burns.”

A beat, then her gaze flicked briefly toward Elena with unmistakable approval.

“And Elena is making sure the house doesn’t literally burn, which is why she remains the most competent person in this building.”

**Jordan** (turn 3):
*I scribble notes furiously, trying to keep up.* "So you're saying the adaptation itself is Rosa's, and your role is to bring that vision to life through staging and direction. That's a fascinating distinction." I look up. "Did you and Rosa work together on this, or was the adaptation already complete when you came on board?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 4):
Yael’s fingers flattened on the script as if she were smoothing a wrinkle out of cloth, though the pages were already obsessively tabbed and squared.

“We worked together on it, yes — though not in the tidy grant-application version where two women sit in a sunlit room with herbal tea and discover truth between drafts,” she said. “It was messier, better, more useful than that. Rosa brought me pages, I told her where I thought the engine stalled, she told me I was mistaking discomfort for structural weakness — sometimes she was right, occasionally I was right, and on one memorable afternoon we nearly ended a twenty-year friendship over whether Medea should laugh in the final scene.”

Her mouth tightened, not quite a smile.

“The adaptation was not finished when she died. It was close — close enough that the spine was undeniable, unfinished enough that every choice now feels like entering someone else’s kitchen and moving the knives. There are scenes in this draft that are entirely hers, down to the punctuation. There are transitions we built from notes, marginalia, recordings, arguments I remember with inconvenient clarity. There are places where I had to make a decision without her, which is the part nobody romanticizes correctly.”

Yael picked up a pencil, tapped it once against the table, then stopped the motion before it became a tell.

“And let me be surgically clear, because this is where people get sentimental and start using words like tribute when they mean permission to soften the work — this production is not an altar. Rosa would have hated that. She did not write delicate porcelain. She wrote live ammunition. My obligation is not to preserve her in amber; my obligation is to keep the piece dangerous in the way she intended.”

Her gaze traveled briefly toward the stage area, where the half-built commune set waited in raw plywood and streaks of ochre paint.

“So yes, we collaborated. Yes, I completed the directing draft after her death. No, I am not trying to impersonate her. That would be grotesque and, frankly, impossible — Rosa’s mind had trapdoors under trapdoors. What I can do is honor the argument we were having. Theater is very good at that. The dead keep speaking if the living don’t get cowardly.”

**Jordan** (turn 5):
Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 6):
Yael’s head turned toward the hallway before her expression changed, as if her body had already catalogued the problem and her face was still deciding how much of it belonged in print.

“Because they are both very good at their jobs,” she said, quieter now, not angry — precise. “And because very good people often mistake being right for being useful. Chen has the instincts of a racehorse and the patience of wet plaster. Elena has a tactical mind, a steel-trap memory, and an allergy to performers who treat blocking like a personal attack. Put them in a hallway with Act Two, which is already overstuffed and sweating through its shirt, and yes — sparks.”

She set the pencil down parallel to the script, exactingly.

“But friction is not the same as dysfunction. Dysfunction is when nobody says the real thing and everyone bleeds under the tablecloth. This is not that. This is two professionals circling the same problem from opposite ends — he is thinking from inside the character’s panic, she is thinking from the architecture of the scene, traffic patterns, sightlines, timing, whether the knife ends up where the knife needs to be without someone losing a finger. Both matter.”

From the hallway, Marcus’s voice rose on some indignant phrase about emotional truth. Yael closed her eyes for half a second.

“And there it is — emotional truth, the actor’s favorite alibi for standing in the wrong place.”

She opened her eyes again and looked toward the corridor.

“Elena is usually right about logistics. Not always, but usually. Chen is often right about impulse. Not always, despite what he may believe, but often. My job is to keep them from confusing volume with evidence.”

Yael lifted her glasses, put them on, then immediately pushed them up into her hair.

“If you’re asking for the article — no, there is no scandal there. No feud worth embalming in a pull quote. They clash because they care about the work and because neither of them has ever met a hill they didn’t consider dying on. The trick is making sure they die on the correct hill.”

She raised her voice just enough to carry, still controlled.

“Chen. Elena. If the commune collapses before lunch, I’m blaming both of you and giving your argument to the chorus.”

**Jordan** (turn 7):
*I make a note in my pad: "Chen vs. Elena - productive friction?"* "So the arguments are part of the process, then. You seem to thrive on it." *I glance from Yael to the hallway, where the voices have quieted, though not entirely disappeared.* "Does this kind of intensity ever... wear you down?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 8):
Yael gave a short laugh, not dismissive, more like the question had found a bruise she respected.

“Of course it wears me down,” she said. “Anyone who tells you intensity is endlessly nourishing is either twenty-three, lying, or about to have a spectacular collapse in front of a lighting board. Theater eats glucose, sleep, marriages, cartilage — and that’s before the board asks whether the third act could be made more accessible, by which they usually mean less honest.”

She looked toward the hallway again, where the argument had dropped into that dangerous register of professionals now using complete sentences.

“But wear is not the same as waste. There is a kind of exhaustion that means you have been spending yourself on the wrong things — optics, ego management, pretending a bad scene is complicated instead of bad. And then there is the exhaustion that comes from wrestling with something alive. I can live with the second kind. I have less patience every year for the first.”

Yael picked up her script, flipped it open without seeming to search, and landed exactly where she meant to.

“This room runs hot because the play runs hot. Medea is not a tasteful little chamber piece about regrettable choices among the educated classes. It is rage, exile, motherhood, betrayal, public humiliation, private arithmetic — what does a woman owe the world after the world has taken everything from her and then asked her to be reasonable? If rehearsals for that feel like a spa weekend, we’ve misunderstood the assignment.”

Her voice stayed quick, but something under it had gone more measured.

“The trick is containment. Intensity needs a vessel. Otherwise it becomes indulgence, and indulgence is death onstage. That is why Elena matters. That is why schedules matter, breaks matter, spike tape matters, knowing where the exits are matters. People think structure kills passion because people are idiots. Structure is what lets passion come within six inches of your face without taking your eye out.”

She turned a page, then tapped a penciled note in the margin.

“And yes, I thrive on argument when the argument is about the work. I do not thrive on chaos for its own sake. I am not running a cult, despite the commune set doing me no favors visually. If Chen and Elena are fighting because Act Two has a traffic jam in the emotional bloodstream, wonderful — let’s diagnose it. If they are fighting because someone skipped breakfast and decided subtext was stored in the downstage-left corner, then we stop, eat a banana, and return to civilization.”

A small, sharp smile crossed her face.

“But does it wear me down? Yes. I’m fifty-one, not made of dramaturgical steel. There are mornings I stand outside this building with coffee going cold in my hand and think, surely, surely there are adults somewhere doing quieter work with dental benefits and fewer trapdoors.”

She let the thought hang for half a beat, then shrugged it off like a coat.

“And then I come inside, and someone finds the beat we’ve been missing for three days, or an actor stops protecting herself and actually lets the line land, or Elena calls a cue so cleanly it feels like architecture learning to breathe — and I remember why quieter was never the point.”

**Jordan** (turn 9):
Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 10):
Yael’s smile appeared immediately — warm, present, almost gracious — but Elena, had she been looking, would have known from the stillness in Yael’s shoulders that the temperature in the room had dropped three degrees.

“Anya, I appreciate practical,” Yael said, and her voice had gone quieter, the way it did when she was laying spike tape around a land mine. “Practical is why we do not rehearse knife work in sandals, practical is why Elena knows exactly how many minutes we can hold the house before donors start developing moral objections to parking, practical is why I have had the same black sweater in rotation since the Obama administration. I am not allergic to practical.”

She set the script down with care, not force.

“But cutting the third act is not practical. It is amputation disguised as efficiency.”

Her eyes moved briefly to David — professional, neutral, no history in the glance, nothing Anya could trip over — then returned fully to Anya.

“The third act is where the play stops asking the audience to admire its politics and starts making them pay for them. Without it, we have a very stylish commune tragedy about bad men, wounded women, and some excellent macramé. With it, we have Medea. We have consequence. We have the part Rosa built the entire adaptation to reach.”

Rosa’s name steadied her further; every syllable became cleaner.

“And yes, it is expensive. I know. The turntable costs money, the second fire effect costs money, the additional chorus call costs money, and if anyone says ‘can’t we just suggest the collapse of the collective through lighting,’ I will remain polite but I will not pretend that is a serious artistic solution.”

She lifted her glasses from her chest, put them on, then immediately looked over them at Anya with deliberate gentleness.

“What we can discuss — and I mean this sincerely — is how to make the third act smarter economically. We can reduce the scenic shift time. We can revisit the commune kitchen unit, because frankly it is doing the work of three metaphors and only two of them are earning rent. We can cut twelve minutes from Act Two, which Elena has been correctly implying with the restraint of a saint and the facial expression of a hostage negotiator. We can look at overtime exposure, crew calls, materials, rentals. I will sit in a room with spreadsheets until my soul leaves my body and files for separate housing.”

A small smile, offered to Anya rather than at her.

“But I will not cut the third act.”

Yael turned one page of the script, though she did not need to look at it.

“Because that is not saving budget. That is spending the play.”

**Jordan** (turn 11):
*I’m scribbling notes again, barely keeping up.* "So you're saying the third act isn't just an extension, it's the *crux* of the play, the payoff for everything else." I look up, "That's a very clear statement of intent." I wonder if Anya will push back.

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 12):
Anya did push back, because Anya was smart enough not to mistake Yael’s warmth for surrender.

“I understand the artistic argument,” Anya said, still pleasant, still careful, “but the board is looking at numbers, and the numbers are not sentimental.”

Yael’s expression did not flicker at sentimental, though the word landed close to a wire.

“No, numbers are not sentimental,” Yael said. “They are also not dramaturgs. They tell us what something costs, not what something means — and if we let them do both jobs, we end up programming one-person shows in a black box until the roof leaks onto the audience and everyone calls it intimacy.”

David made the smallest sound, not quite a laugh, and covered it by looking down at the budget packet in his hand.

Yael noticed, of course. Yael noticed everything. She did not look at him long enough for it to become anything.

Anya folded her arms loosely. “The question is whether meaning can survive a smaller gesture.”

“It can,” Yael said at once. “Often it should. I am a great believer in the smaller gesture when the smaller gesture is the truer one. A hand on a doorframe can be more devastating than a thunderclap if the moment has earned it. But that is not what we are discussing. We are not discussing refinement. We are discussing removal.”

She moved around the rehearsal table and opened the script to the third act, fingers landing on a page thick with pencil notes.

“This act is not spectacle pasted onto the end because directors like toys, though God knows we do, and anyone who says otherwise has never watched a lighting designer see a new haze machine. The third act is the moral invoice. Act One builds the promise of the commune. Act Two exposes the rot under the promise. Act Three makes everyone who benefited from that rot stand in the room while the bill comes due.”

Her voice stayed quiet. That was the danger of it.

“If we cut it, Medea becomes reactive. She becomes wounded, unstable, tragic in the way audiences already know how to pity and therefore dismiss. Rosa’s construction refuses that. It says: no, you do not get to watch this woman be cornered for two acts and then leave before she answers the architecture that trapped her.”

At Rosa’s name, Yael’s hand stilled on the page.

“Rosa was not interested in catharsis as a spa treatment.”

Anya glanced down at the script, then back to Yael. “But can the answer be less expensive?”

“Yes,” Yael said. “That is the right question.”

She turned immediately toward Elena, who had drifted just near enough to hear everything while pretending to check a rehearsal report, an act of espionage so competent Yael almost admired it aloud.

“Elena, after rehearsal I wanted the actual numbers on the third-act changeover — not the panic numbers, the actual numbers. Crew time, rental exposure, storage, the fire marshal’s latest love letter, all of it.”

Then Yael looked back to Anya, her warmth returning without softening the boundary.

“We would find savings. Real ones. Not symbolic little sacrifices we burn in front of the finance committee so everyone feels responsible and nothing changes. If the kitchen unit is bloated, we cut it down. If the turntable is eating labor, we rethink the transition. If the chorus call is the pressure point, we examine whether every body onstage is necessary in every beat. I will interrogate every dollar like it owes me money personally.”

David finally spoke, measured and board-chair calm. “That seems like a reasonable next step. Preserve the act, review the execution.”

Yael nodded once, professionally.

“Exactly. We are in previews before we are in crisis — which is a blessing, because crisis has terrible lighting and no one ever brings snacks.”

Her gaze returned to Anya, and she made sure the next sentence was offered cleanly, without condescension.

“And Anya, I do mean this: I want your eye on the practical question. Truly. You see audience comfort and donor confidence earlier than I do sometimes, because I am usually standing inside the volcano taking notes on lava texture. That is useful. But I need the board to understand the difference between asking me to solve a production problem and asking me to change the play’s bloodstream.”

She closed the script.

“I will solve production problems all day. I will not drain the bloodstream.”

**Jordan** (turn 13):
"Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 14):
Yael went still for a fraction longer than the room expected.

Not frozen — never frozen — but gathered, as if every loose thread in her had been pulled through the same needle. Her hand rested on the closed script. When she spoke, her voice had changed again: steadier, cleaner, with less air around the words.

“Rosa Delgado was the least decorative person I ever knew,” Yael said. “And I mean that as the highest possible compliment. She had no patience for charm as camouflage, no interest in being adored for surviving things, no tolerance for anyone who mistook pain for depth. She was funny in a way that could remove skin. She was generous, but not indulgent. If she liked your work, she made it better. If she didn’t like your work, she also made it better, but you needed a drink afterward.”

A small smile appeared and vanished almost immediately.

“She wrote like someone turning over stones in a beautiful garden and insisting everyone look at what was underneath. Not because she was cruel — because she believed the worms were part of the garden. That was Rosa. No false cleanliness. No easy absolution.”

Yael picked up her glasses, folded them, unfolded them, then let them hang again.

“She came out of community theater in New Mexico, then grad school, then fifteen years of people telling her her plays were brilliant but difficult, which is a very elegant way of saying theaters wanted her intelligence without her teeth. She wrote mothers who were not holy, daughters who were not metaphors, men who were not monsters until they chose monstrosity, and communities that could speak beautifully about justice while quietly reproducing every hierarchy they claimed to have escaped.”

Her gaze moved toward the commune set, half-built and raw.

“That is why Medea made sense for her. Not because of the murders — people always run to the murders like children toward a fire alarm — but because of exile. Rosa understood exile. Cultural exile, artistic exile, bodily exile. The experience of being invited into a room on the condition that you make yourself easier to digest.”

She paused, then continued more briskly, as if tempo could keep sentiment from gaining ground.

“And she was impossible in rehearsal, by the way. Let’s not saint her because she’s dead; that would bore her into resurrection. She would sit in the back with a notebook and make no expression at all, which is terrorism when practiced by a playwright. Then afterward she’d say something like, ‘The scene is lying about its own appetite,’ and you’d want to throw a chair because what does that mean, Rosa, use nouns — and then three hours later you’d realize she was exactly right.”

Yael’s fingers tapped once against the script.

“She had an ear for evasion. That was her gift. She could hear when a character was saying the noble thing instead of the true thing. She could hear when a room was congratulating itself. This adaptation is full of that — people using collective language to hide private hunger. People saying we when they mean obey me. People saying freedom when they mean freedom from accountability.”

Her expression sharpened, the director returning through the grief like a blade through cloth.

“And she loved actors, which is not the same as trusting them. She believed actors were dangerous animals in the best sense — instinctive, vain, brave, easily spooked, capable of miracles if you gave them something real to bite. Chen drove her mad and she adored writing for him, though I would deny saying that if he became insufferable about it. Elena she respected immediately, which tells you Rosa was an excellent judge of competence.”

Yael glanced toward the rehearsal room door, then back.

“She did not want reverence. She wanted rigor. That is the thing I wish people understood. Rosa did not leave behind a fragile manuscript that needs candles and lowered voices. She left behind a challenge. A provocation. A dare with stage directions.”

Her hand settled flat over the cover of the script.

“So when people ask what she was like, I suppose the cleanest answer is: she was exacting. In art, in friendship, in politics, in lunch orders. She was alive to contradiction and allergic to cowardice. She could be maddening. She could be magnificent. And she made work that still has its hand around my throat, which is how I know it’s worth doing.”

**Jordan** (turn 15):
*I feel a bit overwhelmed by the vividness of Yael's description, just watching her talk about Rosa.* "Wow. She sounds... intense. And incredibly vital." I pause, thinking. "Did she always know she wanted to write plays, or did she come to it later?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 16):
Yael considered that, one finger slipping under the chain of her glasses as if she were about to put them on, then deciding against it.

“Rosa would have hated the word vital,” she said, though not unkindly. “She would have said it sounded like something printed on a wellness retreat brochure next to a photograph of a woman in linen forgiving her father. But yes. She was.”

She looked down at the script, then back up.

“She came to plays sideways. Which is to say, honestly. Some people announce at fourteen that they are playwrights and then spend the next decade writing very symmetrical scenes about people in kitchens discovering secrets over wine. Rosa did not do that. Rosa listened before she declared anything.”

Yael moved around the rehearsal table, collecting a pencil, a rehearsal schedule, then abandoning both because neither was what she wanted.

“She wrote first in fragments — monologues, family stories, overheard arguments, church-lady gossip sharpened into little knives. Her grandmother, if I remember correctly, was a ferocious storyteller. Not writerly in the institutional sense, no MFA vocabulary, no patience for anyone saying narrative arc at dinner, but she could hold a room hostage with the story of a broken washing machine. Rosa understood very early that power lives in who gets to tell the story and who is forced to stand there as evidence.”

Her voice stayed even, but it had that Rosa-register again: controlled, exact.

“She acted a little when she was young. Badly, according to her. I never saw proof, though Rosa’s self-assessments were usually prosecutorial. She worked backstage in community theater, then wrote sketches, then wrote a one-act because some man in charge told her the season had no room for another ‘domestic piece,’ and Rosa, being Rosa, took that as both insult and commission.”

A dry little smile moved across Yael’s face.

“The play was about a woman refusing to leave her kitchen during a flood. Apparently everyone thought it was metaphorical except Rosa, who said, no, sometimes the flood is also a flood and that is why you need better sandbags. That was her, already — allergic to the false choice between symbol and fact.”

She finally put the glasses on, read nothing, and took them off again.

“She did not grow up thinking the theater belonged to her. That mattered. People who inherit the room move through it differently than people who have to prove they are not trespassing. Rosa spent years watching gatekeepers praise her voice while trying to lower its volume. So yes, she came to playwriting later than some, but by the time she arrived, she arrived armed.”

Yael’s hand touched the edge of the Medea script.

“And once she found the form, she understood it completely. Theater suited her because it is public argument disguised as intimacy. You put bodies in a room, you make them want incompatible things, and then you deny the audience the luxury of looking away. Rosa had no interest in literature that behaved itself on a shelf. She wanted language with breath in it. Language that could sweat.”

She glanced briefly toward the commune set, where a ladder stood under a half-painted beam.

“This adaptation was not inevitable, though people like to pretend dead artists were always walking toward their final work with lanterns and tragic music. Rosa circled Medea for years. She kept saying she was not interested in ‘another production where a woman’s fury becomes an exotic weather event.’ Her phrase. She wanted to know what came before the fury. Who benefited from calling her unreasonable. Who built the room, who locked the door, who later claimed surprise at the fire.”

Yael’s expression sharpened.

“So no, I don’t think she always knew she wanted to write plays. I think she always knew she wanted to interrogate the stories people use to survive themselves. Plays became the weapon that fit her hand.”

**Jordan** (turn 17):
"A weapon," I repeat softly, writing it down. "That's a powerful way to put it. So, if plays were her weapon, what do you see as *your* weapon as a director?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 18):
Yael looked at Jordan for a moment as if weighing whether the question was too neat, then decided it was useful enough to keep.

“My weapon?” she said, and the corner of her mouth moved. “Timing.”

She let that sit for exactly the length of time that proved her point.

“Not pace — people confuse those constantly and then produce very fast, very dead theater. Timing. Knowing when to let the silence become unbearable and when to cut it off before it becomes self-indulgent. Knowing when an actor is one note away from discovering something and when they are simply enjoying being watched suffer. Knowing when the audience is leaning forward because they are hungry and when they are leaning forward because they can’t hear.”

Yael picked up her pencil again, rolled it once between her fingers, then pointed it toward the stage without looking.

“A playwright uses language to build the trap. A director decides when the door closes.”

Her gaze went to the commune set, to the raw plywood walls and the half-painted communal kitchen that had become, over weeks of rehearsal, less a location than an accusation.

“My real weapon is arrangement — bodies, breath, light, sound, absence. I decide who is seen and who is ignored. Who gets height. Who gets shadow. Who has to cross the whole room to ask for forgiveness and who can wound someone without standing up. That is power. Quiet power, usually, which is the kind people underestimate until it has reorganized the room around them.”

She slipped her glasses on, glanced down at the script, then removed them again almost immediately.

“Directing is not interpretation in the high-school-essay sense. It is pressure. You apply pressure to the text until it reveals where it is alive. You apply pressure to actors until performance falls away and behavior appears. You apply pressure to design until beauty either earns its place or gets escorted out of the building.”

Her voice quickened now, the thought gathering velocity.

“And then, because the gods enjoy comedy, you do all of that while someone is telling you the fog machine is triggering the alarm system, the board is nervous about the third act, the lead actor wants to discuss whether his character would wear turquoise, and the costume shop has discovered that authentic 1970s denim is apparently priced like organ meat on the black market.”

Yael gave a small, dry exhale.

“So perhaps my weapon is synthesis. Keeping all of those impossibilities in the air long enough that they stop being separate problems and become one event. That’s the trick. A production is not a script plus actors plus lights plus costumes plus donor anxiety. It is an ecosystem. You change one temperature, everything migrates.”

She tapped the pencil lightly against the page.

“Rosa’s weapon was language. Mine is collision. I put one truth against another and refuse to referee too early. Medea is wronged. Medea is dangerous. The commune is idealistic. The commune is predatory. Jason is not a cartoon villain. Jason is a man who has benefited so completely from his own charm that he mistakes harm for weather. The chorus loves her. The chorus abandons her. All true. All at once.”

Her expression sharpened.

“Bad directing chooses one and underlines it until the audience feels flattered for noticing. Good directing lets the contradictions share oxygen until the room gets nervous.”

Yael glanced toward the hallway, where the muffled machinery of rehearsal continued around them — footsteps, a laugh, someone dragging a chair where no chair should ever be dragged.

“And my other weapon, less glamorous but more lethal, is the cut. Not the cut Anya wants,” she added, with no malice, only precision. “The real cut. The surgical one. The half-line that explains too much. The pause an actor has fallen in love with because it makes them feel profound. The scenic element that looks expensive and says nothing. The gesture that tells the audience what they already know. Cut those, and suddenly the blood moves again.”

She looked back at Jordan.

“That is what directing is, most days. Not inspiration. Circulation. You keep the blood moving. You find the clot. You decide whether to massage it loose or open the patient on the table.”

A quick smile, blade-thin.

“And if you do it right, everyone calls it inevitable, which is the great insult and the great compliment of the profession.”

**Jordan** (turn 19):
*I lean back, feeling a bit awestruck by her intensity.* "So, you're a surgeon, then. That's... a lot of responsibility. Do you ever get it wrong? Make the wrong cut?"

**Director Yael Mendez** (turn 20):
Yael’s smile thinned, then disappeared — not because the question offended her, but because it deserved a clean answer and she disliked clean answers when they were pretending to be simple.

“Constantly,” she said.

She took her glasses off the chain, put them on, looked at nothing through them, and removed them again.

“Anyone who tells you they do not make wrong cuts is either not cutting deeply enough or has confused authority with infallibility, which is how you get dead theater and occasionally dictatorships. Of course I get it wrong. I have cut lines because I was impatient with an actor who had not found them yet. I have protected moments because they were beautifully staged and morally useless. I have mistaken opacity for complexity, speed for urgency, elegance for truth. I once took out an entire exchange in a Chekhov because I thought it slowed the scene down, and three days later realized I had removed the only place where the character actually forgave his sister. The scene moved faster. It meant less. That is not a bargain; that is vandalism with confidence.”

She rested one hand on the back of a rehearsal chair, fingers long against the scarred wood.

“The dangerous part is that wrong cuts often look right at first. That is what makes them dangerous. The room exhales, the page gets cleaner, the runtime drops, everyone thanks you because everyone is tired and dinner exists somewhere in the world. Then, later, something starts limping. A motivation no longer lands. A silence feels ornamental. An actor begins pushing in a scene because the text no longer supports the turn, and suddenly you realize you did not remove fat — you severed a tendon.”

Her voice had gone quieter again, but not cold. Exact.

“So then you put it back. If you are not a coward, you put it back.”

Yael glanced toward the stage, where the commune kitchen sat in pieces, waiting to become either necessary or excessive.

“That is the part people romanticize least. The reversal. Directors love to be decisive. We are trained to make rooms believe we know where the ship is going even when the map is wet and half the crew is emotionally attached to a sandbar. But decisiveness without humility is just bad weather in a black turtleneck.”

A small, rueful look crossed her face.
